summary.text: Reduce the coefficient formula modulo \(2\) and pair each valid triple satisfying \(m=n(k+1)+(n+1)j\) with \((k+j,k,n-k)\); a binomial-product identity makes the paired weights equal, so every nonfixed pair cancels. At a fixed point \(n=k+j\): if \(j=0\), then \(m=n(n+1)\), while if \(j>0\), the weight is even because another binomial identity exhibits the even central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2j}{j}\) as a factor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge 0}x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1+x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
   =\sum_{m\ge 0}a(m)x^m.
\]
We prove that if the integer \(a(m)\) is odd, then \(m=r(r+1)\) for some nonnegative integer \(r\).

First we extract a convenient expression for the coefficient of \(x^m\). For each fixed \(n\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
(1+x^n)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^{nk},
\]
while the negative-binomial expansion gives
\[
(1+x^{n+1})^{-(n+1)}
 =\sum_{j\ge 0}(-1)^j\binom{n+j}{j}x^{(n+1)j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1+x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
 =\sum_{k=0}^n\sum_{j\ge0}
 (-1)^j\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
 x^{n(k+1)+(n+1)j}.
\]
Thus, if we define
\[
S_m=\{(n,k,j)\in\mathbb N^3:
       k\le n\text{ and }m=n(k+1)+(n+1)j\},
\]
then
\[
a(m)=\sum_{(n,k,j)\in S_m}
 (-1)^j\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}. \tag{1}
\]
This is a finite sum: from the defining equation of \(S_m\) we have
\(n\le n(k+1)\le m\), so only \(0\le n\le m\) can occur; for fixed \(n\), there are only the finitely many choices \(0\le k\le n\), and then \(j\) is uniquely determined if it exists.

We shall study (1) modulo \(2\). In characteristic two, \((-1)^j=1\), so
\[
a(m)\equiv
\sum_{(n,k,j)\in S_m}\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
\pmod 2. \tag{2}
\]

We now define an involution on the triples in \(S_m\). Put
\[
T(n,k,j)=(k+j,\ k,\ n-k). \tag{3}
\]
The assumption \(k\le n\) ensures that all three coordinates on the right are nonnegative. Write
\[
(n',k',j')=(k+j,k,n-k).
\]
Then \(k'=k\le k+j=n'\), and a direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
n'(k'+1)+(n'+1)j'
 &= (k+j)(k+1)+(k+j+1)(n-k)\\
 &= nk+n+nj+j\\
 &= n(k+1)+(n+1)j\\
 &=m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(T(n,k,j)\in S_m\). Applying \(T\) a second time yields
\[
T(k+j,k,n-k)
 =\bigl(k+(n-k),\ k,\ (k+j)-k\bigr)
 =(n,k,j),
\]
so \(T\) is indeed an involution of \(S_m\).

The two binomial products attached to a triple and its image have the same parity; in fact, they are equal as integers. Namely,
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
 =\binom{k+j}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k}. \tag{4}
\]
To see this directly, both sides equal
\[
\frac{(n+j)!}{k!\,(n-k)!\,j!}.
\]
The right side of (4) is exactly the weight associated to the transformed triple: since
\[
n'=k+j,\qquad k'=k,\qquad j'=n-k,
\]
we have
\[
\binom{n'}{k'}\binom{n'+j'}{j'}
 =\binom{k+j}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k}.
\]
Therefore every two-element orbit of \(T\) contributes twice the same residue to (2), and hence contributes zero modulo \(2\). It remains only to analyze fixed points of \(T\).

A triple \((n,k,j)\) is fixed by \(T\) precisely when
\[
n=k+j; \tag{5}
\]
the third-coordinate equality \(j=n-k\) is equivalent to the same condition. There are two cases.

First suppose \(j=0\). Then (5) gives \(n=k\). Substituting into the equation defining \(S_m\), we get
\[
m=n(k+1)+(n+1)j=n(n+1). \tag{6}
\]
Thus a fixed point with \(j=0\) can occur only when \(m\) has the required form.

Now suppose \(j>0\). At a fixed point, \(n=k+j\), so its weight in (2) is
\[
\binom{k+j}{k}\binom{k+2j}{j}. \tag{7}
\]
We claim that this integer is even. The factorial formula, or an elementary double-counting identity, gives
\[
\binom{k+j}{k}\binom{k+2j}{j}
 =\binom{k+2j}{k}\binom{2j}{j}. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, both sides of (8) equal
\[
\frac{(k+2j)!}{k!\,j!\,j!}.
\]
For every positive integer \(j\), the central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2j}{j}\) is even. To prove this, Pascal's identity gives
\[
\binom{2j}{j}
 =\binom{2j-1}{j-1}+\binom{2j-1}{j}.
\]
By binomial symmetry,
\[
\binom{2j-1}{j}=\binom{2j-1}{(2j-1)-j}
=\binom{2j-1}{j-1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\binom{2j}{j}=2\binom{2j-1}{j-1},
\]
which is even. Equation (8) therefore proves that the fixed-point weight (7) is even whenever \(j>0\).

We can now finish the argument. Assume, toward a contradiction, that \(m\) is not of the form \(r(r+1)\) for any \(r\ge0\). Partition the finite set \(S_m\) into the orbits of the involution \(T\). Every orbit with two distinct elements has total weight zero modulo \(2\), by (4). For a one-element orbit, its triple is fixed. The case \(j=0\) is impossible under our assumption, because it would imply (6). Every remaining fixed point has \(j>0\), and its weight is zero modulo \(2\) by (7)–(8) and the evenness of the central binomial coefficient. Thus every orbit contributes zero modulo \(2\), and (2) implies
\[
a(m)\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
Therefore \(a(m)\) is even whenever \(m\) is not of the form \(r(r+1)\). Taking the contrapositive, if \(a(m)\) is odd, then there exists \(r\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
\boxed{m=r(r+1)}.
\]
This is the desired assertion.
